facts.t: Water sources of the 62 federal schemes: 35 take water straight from rivers, 20 from dam reservoirs, 5 from lakes and 2 from boreholes.
84% of public schemes depend on pumps, many of them old and energy-hungry; 19% were designed for sprinklers, which farmers had not adopted.
About three schemes accounted for 90% of the area irrigated on public schemes; Kano River Phase I and the Hadejia Valley alone gave 73% of the 29,140 ha on federal schemes.
Larger dams lasted longer partly because they were over-designed and under-used; many dams were built with hydropower units that were never installed.
Waterlogging and salinity were reported at Kano River Phase I, South Chad and Bakolori, and flooding at schemes south of latitude 9° N.
Water charges (₦500–10,500 per ha a season) were far below the diesel cost of pumping, and effective water users’ associations were rare.
The review recommended no new public irrigation projects until existing schemes were well used and self-sustaining.
Fadama (floodplain) irrigation potential was put at 2.04 million ha.

potential.t: Profitable groundwater irrigation potential is 5.04 million ha for a rice–okra rotation (53% of it solar-powered) and 2.83 million ha for maize–cowpea (91% solar).
95% of the rice–okra area and 93% of the maize–cowpea area is in central and northern states; Yobe, Kebbi and Sokoto have the most solar-profitable land.
Over its life, irrigating one hectare cost about US$3,704 with solar pumps against US$5,080 with diesel.
FAO AQUASTAT puts the area equipped for irrigation at about 0.33 million ha, of which about 67,000 ha use groundwater.
Only 11–14% of farmers surveyed in 2019 in the north had formal credit, a major barrier to buying pumps.
In the Niger basin, Nigeria irrigated about 82,620 ha from 94 intakes in 2005, withdrawing 847 million m³ a year.
Nigeria’s fadama systems mainly draw on shallow groundwater, while public full-control schemes have been largely abandoned.

plans.t: SPIN (Sustainable Power and Irrigation in Nigeria), proposed with World Bank support: rehabilitate about 40,000 ha of irrigation below existing dams and improve the safety of 10–20 existing dams. No new dams. Component budgets are indicative (US$30m institutions, US$350m irrigation, US$100m dam safety, US$20m management).
National goal cited in the SPIN framework: irrigation and drainage services on 500,000 ha by 2030.

TRIMING II, proposed for the Benue basin: a programme of about US$600 million over 6–7 years built on participatory irrigation management, comparing the Dadin Kowa and Guyuk (about 32,000 ha) schemes.
The Niger Basin Authority aimed to raise irrigation in the basin from 265,000 ha to 1.5 million ha by 2025, nearly 1 million ha of it in Nigeria.

benue.t: Around Makurdi, the irrigated farming system covers about 23% of the study area. Water comes from the Benue, Katsina-Ala, Mu, Gwer and Guma rivers and from dug and tube wells.
65% of irrigating farmers surveyed lift water with pumps and 35% by hand, on plots of 0.5–2 ha; more than half the water is sometimes wasted.
The Lower Benue RBDA schemes at Makurdi, Katsina-Ala, Jato-Aka, Buruku and Gbagi Ocholi were described as “in crisis” from poor management and missing equipment.
In 2003/04 the Lower Benue RBDA irrigated 70 ha of the 1,170 ha it had developed (11,175 ha planned).

history.t: In the 1970s the Land Resources Development Centre found water supplies poor in the dry season across the Kano Plains, with farmers and herders competing for fadama land, and recommended investigating groundwater irrigation.

Mapping where irrigation is suitable needs soil texture, depth, drainage, salinity and slope layers. Parametric methods such as the one Boka (2021) applied in Ethiopia could be used for Nigeria, but no such map is included here yet.

facts.t: The study screened 54 possible sites of 5 MW or more (23 known, 31 newly found from elevation data), cut them to 12 and then recommended 3 for development: together 410 MW and about 1,795 GWh a year. These are candidate sites from a study, not approved projects.
Sites were scored on financial feasibility (30%), social impacts (20%), technical constraints (15%), multipurpose benefits (15%), environmental impacts (10%) and governance (10%).
The greatest remaining potential is on the Benue and its left-bank tributaries (Donga, Katsina-Ala, Taraba); large dams on the Niger main stem were judged no longer feasible.
In the dry season these rivers would produce only 15–20% of their wet-season power.
Kainji, Jebba and Lagdo (in Cameroon) supplied about 68% of Nigeria’s electricity at the time of the Niger basin study.

benue.t: The Benue is about 1,400 km long and almost entirely navigable in the rainy season; it rises on the Adamawa Plateau in Cameroon and meets the Niger at Lokoja.
Before 1960 its mean flow (about 3,400 m³/s) was larger than the Niger’s at the confluence (about 2,500 m³/s); the ToR notes these figures need updating.
The basin drains 338,200 km² at Lokoja, more than 70% of it in Nigeria, and is home to over 26.5 million people in Nigeria.
Main tributaries: Faro, Gongola, Mayo Kebbi, Taraba, Donga and Katsina-Ala (left bank majors: Faro, Taraba, Donga, Katsina-Ala).
Six NIHSA gauging stations on the Benue (Wurobokki, Lau, Ibi, Katsina-Ala, Umaisha, Makurdi) were reported as mostly vandalised or not working.

Releases from Lagdo Dam in Cameroon flooded communities downstream in 2012, when floods along the Benue and Niger killed 363 people and displaced 2.2 million. Nigeria and Cameroon signed a memorandum on Benue basin consultations on 3 May 2016.
The Master Plan 2013 gives the basin about 192,000 ha of planned irrigation potential and the largest hydropower energy potential of the eight hydrological areas.

niger.t: Nigeria holds 562,372 km² (44%) of the hydrologically active Niger basin; that is 61.5% of Nigeria’s territory.
About 71% of the basin’s people live in Nigeria; the basin had about 94 million people in 2005, projected at 186–384 million by 2050.
About 36 km³ a year enters the lower Niger and about 180 km³ a year reaches the sea, after the Benue and other tributaries join.
The 1970s–80s drought cut rainfall across the basin but runoff fell least over the Benue and the lower Niger.
Irrigation withdrawals upstream already affect Kainji’s power output and the Niger Delta.
Multipurpose dams planned upstream (Kandadji in Niger, Taoussa in Mali, Fomi in Guinea) are expected to reduce inflows to Kainji and Jebba.

g371.v: 1,874 million m³ (1,845 in another table); 48 m high; 1974. Rated good. Instrument records were not made available to the reviewers in January 2004.

g5170.v: 33 million m³; 22 m high. Rated poor: steep downstream slope with gully erosion and no toe drain. Third on the repair priority list.

g1951.v: 930 million m³; 42 m high; 1992. Rated good. A 4 m drop at the end of the stilling basin was eroding the ford to Turawa village.

g1937.v: 142.7 million m³ (121 in another table); 21.5 m high; 1991. Rated good, but no instrument readings had been taken since 1994.

g1947.v: 177 million m³; 19 m high; 1983. Rated good. Past foundation seepage needed a permanent toe-drain solution.

g365.v: 942 million m³; 20 m high; 1983–84. Rated good and recently rehabilitated, yet its irrigation scheme had only 250 ha developed.

g1943.v: 450 million m³; 48 m high; 1976. Rated good. Its two small turbines needed repair or installation.

g10546.v: 22 million m³; 11.75 m high. Rated good. The intake gate support beam needed urgent repair and the reservoir is silting up.

g5196.v: 5 million m³ diversion structure; 1992. Rated good; the access road needed repair.

g6594.v: 70 million m³ (57 in another table); 1992. Rated good; needed an access road and repair of a crater below the flip bucket.

g6612.v: 4.2 million m³; 15 m high. Cause for concern: the spillway failed and was severely eroded in 2003. First on the repair priority list.

g60.v: 15,000 million m³; 78.7 m high; 1968. Rated good; well instrumented and maintained.
The largest reservoir in the Niger basin. Upstream irrigation withdrawals already affect its power output.

g379.v: 3,600 million m³; 40 m high; 1984. Rated adequate. The spillway channel needed urgent rehabilitation (about ₦1 billion); second on the priority list.

g1960.v: 615 million m³; 20 m high; 1982. Rated good, but 29 hydraulic piezometers had not worked for 10 years.
Downstream of Dadin Kowa; supplies irrigation water to the Savannah Sugar estate at Numan. It has provision for hydropower but no equipment installed.

w127960718.v: 15 m high; 1992. Cause for concern: overtopped and breached in 1998. A redesign was awarded but the contractor had not started by March 2004.

g376.v: 2,800 million m³ (1,770 live storage); 42 m high; 1987–88. Rated “good but un-utilised”: the reservoir lay idle with spillway gates permanently open; 34 MW of turbines were planned but not installed.
Designed to irrigate 6,200 ha at Dadin Kowa and 18,800 ha at Guyuk through a diversion weir that was not built; a 2,000 ha “quick-win” scheme was being built under TRIMING.
The ToR gives 14 MW in its description and 40 MW in its table of priority projects.

g1973.v: Completed 1983; 270 million m³. Supplies water to Lagos and Abeokuta and feeds the Lower Ogun irrigation scheme; its 9 MW of hydropower was not fully installed.

g1966.v: Completed 1985; 565 million m³. Water supply and the Middle Ogun irrigation scheme, which had never irrigated any land; 6 MW of hydropower not fully installed.

g1965.v: Completed 1976; 220 million m³ on the Oyi river. Feeds the Kampe scheme, where 100 ha of 1,000 ha developed were irrigated.

nukhunerhaedo.v: Earth dam completed 1993, in poor condition with leakages and a failed upstream slope; its 250 ha scheme was abandoned.

g6596.v: Dam not complete and no irrigation infrastructure downstream.

g7412.v: A multipurpose buffer dam against a possible failure of the natural dam at Lake Nyos in Cameroon; 40 MW, about 2,000 ha of irrigation and water for about 400,000 people.

g5220.v: Planned to irrigate 39,000 ha; 2,000 ha were developed for sprinklers but completion stalled for lack of pumps, generator and pipes.
Facilities dilapidated, no emergency action plan or flood warning, and the dam area is not restricted. A pilot site for the proposed SPIN project, rated moderate risk.

nnakaben.v: On the River Ana at Naka, Gwer West; built in the 1980s, 2 million m³, mainly for Naka town’s water supply. Designed to irrigate 10 ha; farmers now pump onto about 100 ha. Silted and not operational; desilting under way. A pilot site for the proposed SPIN project.

g377.v: Installed capacity 600 MW on the Kaduna River.

xzungeru.v: 700 MW, under construction in 2016, downstream of Shiroro.

gauge-benue-border.v: Lagdo Dam in Cameroon (about 50 km south of Garoua) is the only significant flood-control structure on the Benue. Releases in 2012 flooded communities downstream in Nigeria.

riv-benue.v: About 1,400 km long; drains 338,200 km² at Lokoja, over 70% in Nigeria. Mean flow before 1960 about 3,400 m³/s, more than the Niger’s 2,500 m³/s at the confluence.
Two shortlisted sites on the main stem: Makurdi (290 MW) and Dasin Hausa (120 or 32 MW).

riv-niger.v: Nigeria holds 44% of the active Niger basin, 61.5% of its own territory; about 180 km³ a year reaches the sea.

riv-donga.v: Watershed about 20,000 km²; peak discharge near the Benue about 1,800 m³/s, roughly 20% of Benue flows. Manya (136 MW) was one of three hydropower sites recommended in 2016.

riv-katsinaala.v: Catchment about 23,000 km²; joins the Benue about 40 km east of Makurdi. Bawarku (182 MW) was one of three hydropower sites recommended in 2016.

riv-gongola.v: About 531 km long to the Benue opposite Numan; catchment about 53,000 km². Dadin Kowa and Kiri are its main storages.
